title: The 614th Commandment
hookLine: Emil Fackenheim taught that after the Holocaust, Jews should keep living as Jews
carry: the 614th commandment: keep living as jews
tomorrow: a survivor kept asking God hard questions. why not just stop?

lines: FRIDAY, A FEW MINUTES BEFORE SUNSET.
AFTER EVERYTHING, WHY KEEP DOING THIS?
cards: Friday, a few minutes before sunset. A kitchen with the dishwasher still humming and a grocery bag on the counter. A woman strikes a match and lights two candles, a little crooked in their holders.
She covers her eyes and says the blessing. Nobody else is home. Nobody would know if she skipped it, and some weeks she almost does.

Her grandmother lit candles like these, and her grandmother's mother, in towns that no longer have a Jew in them. So the question sits in the kitchen with her: after everything, why keep doing this at all?
After the darkest years, one thinker heard an answer, and he called it a commandment.

teach.h: SIX HUNDRED AND THIRTEEN, PLUS ONE.
teach.b: Emil Fackenheim, a rabbi and philosopher, spent years with that question after the Holocaust. A gentle word first: this is heavy history, and today stays with the answer, not the horror.
The Talmud says six hundred and thirteen commandments were given to Moses. Fackenheim spoke of one more, a six hundred and fourteenth, heard, he wrote, as a commanding voice out of Auschwitz.
His paraphrase of it: Jews are forbidden to hand Hitler a victory after his death. Don't stop being Jews. Don't despair of God.
Here's the surprise worth telling a friend: his new commandment adds no new ritual. It adds a reason to keep the old ones. Candles on a Friday.
A seder table too small for the cousins. A Hebrew name for a new baby. A joke at the kitchen table in a grandmother's accent.
Ordinary Jewish life, kept going, becomes the answer. Not everyone agreed.
Some Jewish thinkers worried about building Jewish life on a catastrophe instead of on Sinai and on joy. Fackenheim's reply, in effect, was that the joy is the point: a living people, not a memorial.

It echoes Moses at the end of Deuteronomy, setting life and death before the people and saying, "therefore choose life." So the woman in the kitchen isn't keeping a museum. She is choosing life, in a crooked candle.

how: Jewish families light Shabbat candles on Friday before sunset, covering their eyes for the blessing; Fackenheim's teaching is often cited to say that keeping such ordinary practices is itself a response to the Holocaust.

o: build memorials so the Holocaust is never forgotten
keep all six hundred thirteen rules without exception
keep Jewish practice going as the answer to catastrophe

games.q: the commandment of one more — tap the pairs.
p: spoke of a six hundred and fourteenth
a reason, not a new ritual

s: keeping Jewish life going means keeping every rule perfectly
Fackenheim's point is to keep living as Jews at all: candles, seders, names, joy. one practice kept is living it.
the Talmud counts six hundred and thirteen commandments given to Moses
Makkot 23b gives that count. Fackenheim spoke of one more.
every Jewish thinker agreed with Fackenheim
some worried about building Jewish life on catastrophe instead of on Sinai and joy.

games.q: your cousin says being Jewish now is mostly about remembering the Holocaust. by Fackenheim's lesson, what's the fuller answer?
o: remembering matters, but his commandment is to live: candles, seders, names, joy.
he's right: after the Holocaust, memory became the whole of Jewish life.
the Holocaust shouldn't shape how Jews live today at all.
games.why: Fackenheim's six hundred and fourteenth commandment asks Jews to keep living as Jews, and not to despair of God or the world. memory, yes; a memorial, no.

practice: Choose one small practice your family keeps, or one you've met on this path: a blessing before food, touching the mezuzah, the words over the candles.

For the sit, do its first piece slowly now: touch the doorframe, hold the cup, or say its opening line out loud. If none fits you, name a practice someone before you kept, and hold their name with it.

wordCard.voice: Keep living Jewishly: Fackenheim's answer to catastrophe. Not a new ritual; a reason to keep the old ones, and to keep them with joy.

carryVoice: Your line: the six hundred and fourteenth commandment, keep living as Jews. A crooked candle on a Friday counts. See you tomorrow.
